quiz.q: A program spends 30% of its time in a function. You speed that function up by 5×. By Amdahl's Law, what is the overall speedup?
Halving supply voltage approximately divides dynamic power by:
quiz.explain: Dynamic power ~ V² × f. Halving V cuts V² by 4. But lower V also halves f, so total power scales as V³ — roughly an 8× reduction.

quiz.q: Which mean is correct for summarizing SPEC speedup ratios?
quiz.explain: Geometric mean is independent of the reference machine — required for normalized speedups.

quiz.q: Doubling the area of a die typically:
choices: More than doubles cost per die
quiz.explain: Yield drops exponentially with defects per die, and dies-per-wafer halves. Combined effect is ~3-4× cost increase.

quiz.q: Dark silicon emerged because:
choices: Transistors got too small to switch reliably
Voltage scaling stalled while transistor density kept doubling
Software couldn't use all the cores
Wires became more resistive than transistors
quiz.explain: Post-2005, Dennard scaling broke: density doubled per node but per-transistor power didn't fall proportionally, so total chip power would balloon. Result: power-gate part of the chip.

quiz.q: AMAT for a system with L1 hit time 2 ns, L1 miss rate 5%, L2 hit time 10 ns, L2 miss rate 1%, memory penalty 100 ns:
Which is NOT one of the original 3 Cs of cache misses?
quiz.explain: Coherence is the 4th C — multicore-specific. The original 3 are compulsory, capacity, conflict.

quiz.q: Why is write-back almost always preferred for L1 caches?
choices: It doesn't need a dirty bit
quiz.explain: Write-back batches writes via dirty-line eviction; write-through hits memory on every store, saturating bandwidth.

quiz.q: RRIP replacement is preferred over LRU because:
choices: It uses less hardware than LRU
It is resistant to scan/streaming workloads that thrash LRU
quiz.explain: RRIP uses re-reference distance prediction; LRU promotes one-time-use lines and gets thrashed by databases and streaming.

quiz.q: VT-x and AMD-V solve which classical x86 virtualization problem?
choices: Sensitive instructions that don't trap when run by guest
quiz.explain: Classical x86 had ~17 sensitive-but-not-privileged instructions, breaking pure virtualization. VT-x adds a non-root mode where these can be trapped.

quiz.q: Which dependence cannot be eliminated by register renaming?
quiz.explain: RAW is a true (flow) dependence; the consumer needs the producer's value. WAR/WAW are name dependences and disappear with renaming.

quiz.q: The Reorder Buffer enables:
quiz.explain: ROB separates execute (out-of-order) from commit (in-order). Architectural state only updates on commit, so exceptions are precise and speculative work can be flushed cleanly.

quiz.q: In a 20-stage pipeline with 95% branch prediction accuracy, the cost of mispredicts is:
choices: Mispredicts don't cost anything in OoO
quiz.explain: 95% accuracy = 1 mispredict per 20 branches; each mispredict wastes ~20 stages of work. With 4-wide issue that's ~80 instructions of wasted work.

quiz.q: SMT (Hyper-Threading) provides throughput gains primarily because:
choices: Each thread gets its own ALU
Independent threads fill execution ports left idle by ILP limits
quiz.explain: A single thread rarely uses all execution ports each cycle; SMT threads share the same OoO core and fill the gaps. ~30% throughput gain for ~5% area overhead.

quiz.q: Itanium (EPIC/VLIW) failed mainly because:
choices: Compilers couldn't find static ILP for irregular code
quiz.explain: VLIW relies entirely on the compiler. Pointer aliasing, dynamic dispatch, and unpredictable cache misses defeated static scheduling. OoO won.

quiz.q: A Return Address Stack (RAS) handles which type of branch?
quiz.explain: RAS is a hardware stack pushed on CALL, popped on RET. Highly accurate for well-nested code; mispredicts on tail calls and longjmp.

quiz.q: In a CUDA warp, if 16 threads take one branch and 16 take the other, the warp:
choices: Serializes both paths with masking, halving throughput
quiz.explain: Warp divergence: hardware executes path A with 16 lanes active, then path B with the inverse mask. Total time = time(A) + time(B).

quiz.q: In the Roofline model, a kernel below the sloped roof is:
quiz.explain: Sloped roof = memory bandwidth × operational intensity. Below it = limited by memory bandwidth. Need to reduce bytes per FLOP (blocking, reuse).

quiz.q: Memory coalescing on a GPU works best when:
choices: Threads in a warp access contiguous addresses within one cache line
Each thread accesses its own unique line
Loads are issued one at a time
quiz.explain: 32 threads accessing contiguous 4-byte words within one 128-byte line = 1 transaction. Random access can balloon to 32 transactions.

quiz.q: Tensor Cores accelerate which workload type?
quiz.explain: Tensor Cores execute MMA: D = A × B + C as a single instruction over a small tile. They target the GEMM-dominated workloads of deep learning.

quiz.q: AVX-512 frequency throttling on Intel Skylake-X happens because:
choices: Wider SIMD draws more power per cycle, exceeding thermal envelope at peak frequency
quiz.explain: Wider SIMD = more switching capacitance per cycle = more power. To stay in TDP, the chip drops 200-400 MHz when AVX-512 is sustained.

quiz.q: In MESI, the Exclusive (E) state's main advantage over Shared (S) is:
choices: Silent transition to Modified on a write — no bus broadcast
quiz.explain: E means 'I'm the only one with this clean copy.' On a write you can go to M without broadcasting because nobody else needs invalidation.

quiz.q: Snooping coherence doesn't scale past ~16-32 cores because:
choices: Bandwidth scales O(N²) since every transaction must be broadcast
Coherence state machines run out of states
quiz.explain: On a shared bus or ring, every transaction is seen by every cache. With N cores, traffic is N × per-core rate — bus saturates.

quiz.q: On ARM (a weak memory model), implementing a lock requires:
choices: Nothing extra — ARM is sequentially consistent
Acquire/release barriers (DMB instructions) at lock and unlock
quiz.explain: ARM allows most reorderings; explicit barriers are needed to prevent reordering across the lock boundary. C++11 acquire/release maps to DMB.

quiz.q: False sharing is fixed by:
choices: Padding so each thread's data lands on a separate cache line
quiz.explain: Pad with alignas(64) (or 128 for Apple) so writes don't share cache lines. Better still, use thread-local storage and reduce at the end.

quiz.q: On a NUMA system, accessing memory on another socket vs local:
choices: Costs roughly 2× more in latency due to inter-socket traversal
quiz.explain: Typical: local ~80ns, remote ~150-200ns. Software optimizes via numactl, thread pinning, NUMA-aware allocation.

quiz.q: PUE of 1.1 vs 2.0 indicates:
choices: 1.1 has 10% overhead, 2.0 has 100% overhead — 1.1 is much more efficient
quiz.explain: PUE = total facility power / IT power. 1.1 → only 10% lost to cooling/distribution; 2.0 → as much non-compute as compute power.

quiz.q: Why is MapReduce well-suited to WSCs?
choices: Independent tasks tolerate worker failures and run on data-local nodes
quiz.explain: At scale, machines fail daily. MapReduce reschedules failed tasks transparently and runs Map on the node holding input data.

quiz.q: In a fat-tree (Clos) network, server-to-server communication takes:
choices: Variable hops depending on rack location
quiz.explain: Spine-leaf: every leaf connects to every spine. Any server-to-server is leaf → spine → leaf. Predictable latency, full bisection bandwidth.

quiz.q: In WSC TCO over a 5-year lifecycle, dominant cost components are:
quiz.explain: Servers are 50-60% of capex. Electricity is the dominant opex. Over 5 years, depreciated servers ≈ power costs — together ~60-70% of TCO.

quiz.q: Modern x86 cores internally:
choices: Decode CISC into RISC-like micro-ops and execute on a RISC-style OoO backend
Compile x86 to RISC-V at boot
quiz.explain: Since Pentium Pro, x86 has been a CISC ISA over a RISC-style internal core. Decoders crack each x86 instruction into 1-4 micro-ops.

quiz.q: Which addressing mode is unique to x86-64 (vs MIPS/ARM)?
choices: Base + index×scale + displacement in one instruction
quiz.explain: x86's ModR/M + SIB encoding can express base + index×scale + displacement in a single instruction. ARM has pieces of this but not all in one mode.

quiz.q: ARM SVE / RISC-V V improve over fixed-width SIMD by:
choices: Vector length is implementation-defined; same binary runs on different SIMD widths
quiz.explain: Scalable vectors let the same code run efficiently on 128-bit and 2048-bit hardware without recompilation. AWS Graviton 3 (256-bit SVE), Fujitsu A64FX (512-bit SVE).

quiz.q: Why are TLBs typically fully associative?
choices: They are small (32-128 entries), so the comparator cost is acceptable
quiz.explain: At ~64 entries, you can afford 64 parallel comparators. Avoids any conflict misses. Larger caches use 4-16-way set associative because comparator cost grows with size.

quiz.q: A 64-byte cache line size has been standard since ~2000 because:
choices: It balances spatial locality, false sharing, and DRAM burst length
It's the largest line that fits in L1
quiz.explain: Tradeoff sweet spot: large enough for good spatial locality and DRAM burst alignment, small enough to limit false sharing in multicore. Apple M-series moved to 128 bytes.

quiz.q: In a 5-stage MIPS pipeline, the load-use hazard requires:
choices: Exactly one stall cycle (or compiler-scheduled independent instruction)
quiz.explain: Load result emerges end of MEM, dependent EX needs it earlier. One unavoidable stall, traditionally filled by compiler scheduling (load delay slot).

quiz.q: Pentium 4's 31-stage NetBurst pipeline failed to outperform shorter pipelines because:
choices: Branch mispredict cost scales with pipeline depth, and power scales superlinearly with frequency
quiz.explain: Deep pipelines amplify mispredict cost. Power scales as ~V²f, but pushing f required higher V. Apple M1's 8-10 stages × 8-wide × 3.2 GHz beats deeper, faster designs on per-thread integer perf.

quiz.q: Branch delay slots were abandoned in MIPS R6 because:
choices: They were a software-visible artifact of one specific pipeline; useless in modern OoO/deep pipelines and a porting nightmare
quiz.explain: In OoO cores, branch prediction fully covers what delay slots used to optimize. They became pure complication for speculation, exception handling, and binary portability. ARM and RISC-V never had them.
